title: Deconstructing Deconstruction
tldr: Deconstruction isn't as high-minded as it appears to be.
md:
---
title: "Deconstructing Deconstruction"
date: 2021-08-23
tldr: "Deconstruction isn't as high-minded as it appears to be."
notion_id: 63f62f54-e815-4778-9313-259fe9982ed3
---

Deconstruction is so hot right now.

I started to hear about it when Joshua Harris mentioned [on instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/B0ZBrNLH2sl/?hl=en) that he was "deconstructing" his faith, and was no longer a Christian:

> *The information that was left out of our announcement is that I have undergone a massive shift in regard to my faith in Jesus. The popular phrase for this is “deconstruction,” the biblical phrase is “falling away.” By all the measurements that I have for defining a Christian, I am not a Christian.*

Since then I've heard of friends and acquaintances that are undergoing the process of "deconstruction". But what does that even mean?

According to a [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deconstruction) on the topic,  "*Deconstruction argues that language, especially in ideal concepts such as truth and justice, is irreducibly complex, unstable, or impossible to determine.*"

To the people (like Harris) that use the term, they seem to imply that they're undergoing a serious reconsideration of values and beliefs once tightly held and assumed to be true.

At face value, it seems like a very healthy thing. However, the traditional, philosophical method of deconstruction evaluates everything (cultural values, philosophical ideas, personal experiences) as equally legitimate, so as the deconstruction begins, once it gets to the objective truth claims about scripture, that gets thrown out as well.

For many people undergoing "deconstruction", the end is usually a wholesale rejection of the truth of the gospel.

Why? 

- Because the culture values things that are in direct opposition to the Apostle Paul's writings.

- Because today's philosophy says that truth should be seen through a personal and cultural lens, and any truth that has been used to perpetuate oppression should be treated as a lie, regardless of how "true" it is.

- Because people have personally experienced hatred from those who uphold scripture as true, and have experienced love and acceptance from those who say it's false.

## The subversion of deconstruction

Although the popular term is "deconstruction", I take issue with that word. Deconstruction seems implies a careful treatment of something, analyzing the parts to then appreciate it in a wider context. In other words, it makes it seem as though the thing being deconstructed still has value.

According to [Merriam-Webster's post](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/deconstruction) on the word,

> *Deconstruction doesn't actually mean "demolition;" instead it means "breaking down" or analyzing something (especially the words in a work of fiction or nonfiction) to discover its true significance, which is supposedly almost never exactly what the author intended.*

The problem with the term is that it has a subversive intent. It breaks things down to get to a conclusion that the author didn't want. When used on scripture it's pretty much making it say whatever you want. Any value that scripture might hold can now be used as a weapon against others, or as a self-help tool for your own ends.

**You decide good and evil.**

The original temptation.

Deconstruction is the tool of the cynic, the person too sophisticated to [cut out pieces of the Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Bible) because he doesn't think it fits. Instead he delegitimizes it through competing truth claims and appeals to cultural norms. It appears to be a careful evaluation, but it really begins with a goal in mind: demolition.

## The need for true "deconstruction"

The bible has been around for quite some time, and man-made teachings are built on top of the core teaching. It's been happening for millennia. Jesus accused the Pharisees of this very thing in Matthew 23:4

> *They tie up heavy, cumbersome loads and put them on other people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.*

This is a natural consequence of studying scripture, making inferences, and studying the inferences and making inferences on top of the inferences.

This is how we end up with church splits over esoteric theological points that require 6 pages of preamble to explain completely ("*Infralapsarian heretic!*")

Whether we call it Deconstruction, Dismantling, Foundational Truth Searching, there needs to be a "back-to-basics" look at Christianity in the lives of each person that has received Jesus' gift of salvation. We need to move past our tribal beliefs and understand what are the core things that make us part of Christ's body.

C.S. Lewis, in his preface to "Mere Christianity", describes Christianity like a great house, with the various rooms being denominations and theologies, and the basic unifying beliefs are the hall of the great house.

> * If I can bring anyone into that hall I shall have done what I attempted. But it is in the rooms, not in the hall, that there are fires and chairs and meals. The hall is a place to wait in, a place from which to try the various doors, not a place to live in. For that purpose the worst of the rooms (whichever that may be) is, I think, preferable. It is true that some people may find they have to wait in the hall for a considerable time, while others feel certain almost at once which door they must knock at. I do not know why there is this difference, but I am sure God keeps no one waiting unless He sees that it is good for him to wait.*

It's important for believers to spend some time in the hall of Christianity to understand its foundational value. If there are certain beliefs that derive from inferences of texts, or a certain interpretation, they do not diminish the value of the whole, they're merely structures built in an attempt to better understand the foundation. However, it should never be mistaken as the foundation itself, because when a man-made doctrine is rejected under the assumption that it is essential to Christianity, there is a risk of rejecting the whole thing.

So let's dismantle the additional structures put on by humans that may or may not be right, to discover the solid rock that is the truth of God's word.

But let's not kid ourselves. That honest search for truth isn't deconstruction.

title: 3 Things to NEVER get better at
tldr: Do your best to be a terrible liar, a horrible mind-reader, and a really bad escape artist.
md:
---
title: "3 Things to NEVER get better at"
date: 2020-12-16
tldr: "Do your best to be a terrible liar, a horrible mind-reader, and a really bad escape artist."
notion_id: 366cc530-0e13-42c6-b166-190b8fc5a62b
---

As we're winding down the year, most people take a look at what they've been able to accomplish, and what they'll aim for in their 2021 new year's resolutions.

![Plant a tree... Have a child... Write a book...](../assets/posts/3-things-to-never-get-better-at/ad463c41-Untitled.png)
*Plant a tree... Have a child... Write a book...*

However, there are some things that we should never get better at, because they avoid real growth. It's like being an expert at the [offline Chrome dinosaur game](https://codepen.io/MysticReborn/embed/rygqao?height=537&theme-id=light&default-tab=result) — it means you're not really getting much done. 

[http://gph.is/29JXvg2](http://gph.is/29JXvg2)

What are these things you should be bad at? Here's three:

# Lying

The truth should be your comfort zone. In business as in personal relationships, the truth eventually comes out. You can't dilute your product forever, you can't bait-and-switch every single time, you can't lie your way out of an uncomfortable conversation and think that your relationship will remain intact.

Abraham Lincoln is credited with saying:

> “You can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.”

Since the truth eventually comes out, lying is playing the short game.
It's a payday loan: immediate benefit at the expense of long-term growth. 
It's avoiding the necessary confrontations that will build you into a better version of yourself.
It's fooling yourself into thinking you're in a better place than you really are.

Even if you reject the moral reasoning for being truthful, there's a good argument to be made about the benefits of honesty from purely a business standpoint. Don't believe me? Here's Steven Covey, talking about the concepts in his book, "The Speed of Trust". 

[https://youtu.be/EId6BsvPwns](https://youtu.be/EId6BsvPwns)

So whether you care about being an upright person, or just want to be successful in life, make sure you stay a terrible liar.

# Mindreading

The term "Emotional Intelligence" is relatively new.

 According to [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotional_intelligence), it's defined as

> ...the capability of individuals to recognize their own emotions and those of others, discern between different feelings and label them appropriately, use emotional information to guide thinking and behavior, and manage and/or adjust emotions to adapt to environments or achieve one's goal(s).

![Although the term first appeared in 1964, it gained popularity in the 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, written by the science journalist Daniel Goleman.](../assets/posts/3-things-to-never-get-better-at/6b1935aa-Untitled.png)
*Although the term first appeared in 1964, it gained popularity in the 1995 book Emotional Intelligence, written by the science journalist Daniel Goleman.*

Emotional intelligence is great. Being able to understand verbal and non-verbal cues to identify emotions in others is a fantastic ability.

You know what's not great? Making the jump to conclusions about the motives of the other person.

You could be right, or you could be completely off-base.

[https://gph.is/1colwVY](https://gph.is/1colwVY)

Mindreading is another evasive skill. It's easier to make assumptions and act on those assumptions than admitting that you COULD have misinterpreted what you saw, and the best thing would be to just ask the other person.

With that said, it's not a guarantee that asking will yield the truth (See point 1 about lying), but there should always be a healthy suspicion in your own abilities to perceive emotion, motive and intention.

Instead of trying to become a better mind-reader, try getting better at listening, interacting, empathizing, and asking directed questions.

If the other person won't open up, choose to believe the person, and act as if it were true. "You're telling me you're fine, and even though it doesn't look like it to me, I'm going to choose to believe you." That way, the onus to be honest is on the other person, not on you to become a better mind-reader.

# The Art of Escape

[http://gph.is/Vx9dyv](http://gph.is/Vx9dyv)

You know what I'm talking about: ghosting, call-screening, convenient and timely sicknesses. It's similar to lying (which can be defined as a kind of verbal escape), but it involves actively avoiding a person, topic, or situation. 

Some people become better escape artists precisely because they're terrible liars. "So I don't have to lie", they think, "I'll just avoid the situation altogether". 

This actually shows a pretty poor ability to manage conflict. "Facing the music" means owning up to your own mistakes, inabilities, ignorance, and may even require putting limits on other people. But instead of answering the phone and saying "I don't want to talk to you right now", "I really can't help with that", or even the dreaded, "I'm sorry", some people decide that it's better to have 57 missed calls, skip out on the next meeting, or conveniently get COVID... for the fourth time.

Escape artists deprive themselves of the opportunity to become better at dealing with disappointment, rejection, or overbearing people. These things will be constants in our lives. As imperfect people, we're always failing to meet someone's standards, so it's better to learn how to deal with that situation, than get better at putting it off.

As we barrel toward 2021, I hope you continue to grow and improve in many, many areas of your life. Just don't get better at those three things.

title: The case for "specialization"
tldr: See what slice of your potential market you understand best, and lean into it. Your specialization might pay off.
md:
---
title: "The case for \"specialization\""
date: 2020-10-21
tldr: "See what slice of your potential market you understand best, and lean into it. Your specialization might pay off."
notion_id: 86dfee45-973a-437d-a0c0-a56e3749dd9b
---

I once lost out on a web project because "the other company that quoted us specializes in websites for franchises".

*What?*

"This is an information website. The only difference is content - a website is a website", I thought. "There's no difference between a 'franchise' website and any other kind of website!"

It's as ridiculous as an architect saying that he "specializes" in building houses for families with small children. 

A house is a house — the only difference is the number of rooms! Whether it's for children or not depends on how you furnish it.

That was a few years ago. With time, I've come to respect my mysterious competition. They understood how to position themselves as unique in a field where there isn't much difference between one kind of product and another (in my case, websites). Although their claim to "specialization" seemed to be marketing fluff in order to close the deal, there are very legitimate reasons to put yourself out in the market as a "specialist" in a specific demographic. 

Here are three:

# You can anticipate specific needs

If our hypothetical architect started getting lots and lots of jobs from families with small children, he may begin to anticipate some requests.

"I'm pretty sure you're going to want a good-sized backyard. Do you want me to factor that into the blueprints?"

"Most of my clients ask for a central kitchen that has access to most parts of the house. Would you like that as well?"

Every niche has specific needs. As someone who has built several websites for church and para-church organizations, I can anticipate certain needs they have, such as the need for accessible audio files, a home page with access to basic information like service times, location and current sermon series. I can even anticipate the kinds of problems they're going to have as the project progresses.

Do I code any differently, or is the actual work any different than if my client were in another industry? 

No.

*What's the benefit, then?*

The client benefits by my specialization and past experience because apart from getting a developer, he's also getting a consultant who can inform him about any blind spots he may have. This can be extremely valuable in the long run, and may even allow a "specialized" developer to charge a premium for that additional expertise.

# You can one-up the industry while staying in-budget

Companies do not all compete with one another. Companies in the same industry compete with one another. In the same way, websites don't have to compete with all the websites that exist, they have to keep up with their competition, and hopefully surpass it.

Having a good understanding of a client's competition allows you to build a solution that lets your client to stand out in their field, while relieving them of the pressure to feel like they need a website that looks like [apple.com](http://apple.com).

It's important to strive for excellence, but if the client is constrained by budget, a good understanding of the industry can give the the insight you need to know what "standing out" will require.

# You can become a point of reference

The pool guy is in touch with the pool supply company, who talks to pool noodle manufacturers. If the pool guy needs help with web design and online marketing, you can become the point of reference in that little business ecosystem, especially if there are concrete sales results attached with your work. By positioning yourself as a "specialist" in pool-related web design and marketing, you give your client a reason to recommend your work to other people in the industry. If we're really honest, it's not exactly a true specialization (since the process isn't different), but by anticipating needs and keeping your clients a step ahead of their own competition, you can become a reference point to everyone associated with that particular client. This, in turn, will reinforce your aura of "expertise".

So see what slice of your potential market you understand best, and lean into it. Invent a specialization for yourself — who knows, it might just pay off.

title: Curation Versus Creation
tldr: Creators offer novelty. Curators offer clarity.
md:
---
title: "Curation Versus Creation"
date: 2020-10-15
tldr: "Creators offer novelty. Curators offer clarity."
notion_id: da17ed2a-5bad-4fc7-b3d2-58c749b0b78e
---

Neil Postman, comparing George Orwell's dystopian world of "1984" and the utopian "Brave New World" of Aldous Huxley, said in his book, "Amusing Ourselves to Death":

> Orwell feared that the truth would be concealed from us. Huxley feared the truth would be drowned in a sea of irrelevance. Orwell feared we would become a captive culture. Huxley feared we would become a trivial culture, preoccupied with some equivalent of the feelies, the orgy porgy, and the centrifugal bumble puppy.

The internet brought us a tidal wave of information.

- 500 hours of video content are uploaded to youtube every minute.

- There are over [1.7 billion](https://www.oberlo.com/blog/internet-statistics#:~:text=Here's%20a%20summary%20of%20the,percent%20of%20the%20global%20population.) websites on the world wide web.

- [3.5 billion](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-internet-users-by-country?tab=chart&time=1990..2016&country=~OWID_WRL) humans use the internet

- People are connected an average of [6 hours per day](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/daily-hours-spent-with-digital-media-per-adult-user)

With so many people online consuming content, the amount of content generated has become staggering. We are flooded by information on the web. It's all there, and for the most part, free.

It seems as though we're living in Huxley's "Brave New World". With so much information, it becomes overwhelming.

As an entrepreneur, it's a double whammy - sometimes it feels like everything that's been created has already been created, and everything interesting you may have to say has already been said.

And it's probably true. 

- There's already [top tier classes](https://online.stanford.edu/free-courses) online that you can take for free

- There is already an incredible amount of interviews, books, articles from great minds around the world putting out higher quality content than you'll ever hope to attain.

- There are already [amazing creators](https://levels.io/) building tools that will make everyone's life easier.

With all this talent, you might as well sit down, shut up and let the professionals work their magic.

What is someone supposed to do?

**Curation.**

Defined as "*the action or process of selecting, organizing, and looking after the items in a collection or exhibition*", curation is always going to be needed, and will be even more needed as content grows. As a curator, you have a chance to go through a vast collection of things, and present it to people in a way that lets them focus **just on what they need**.

# Curation will always be in demand

There's a reason celebrities get paid millions of dollars to put out a tweet recommending one product or another. It's because that person has created a huge following of people that trust his or her opinion. "Well, if this product is good enough for X celebrity, it's good enough for me". They've made that celebrity a kind of curator.

[https://www.goodbooks.io/](https://www.goodbooks.io/) is a great example of a website designed to curate book choices. Who is doing the curating? According to the website, it's "successful people". Who is curating the "successful people"? The web developer.

Is the developer doing anything new, groundbreaking, incredible? Not really. It's a nice-looking, polished site, but there's not really anything new in terms of CONTENT. However, he is providing a service: putting all the book recommendation from "successful people" in one searchable page. And as a reader, that has enormous value.

# Curation has never been easier

That website I just mentioned was built using webflow, a drag-and-drop website creator. Today, with modern tools, you can build out a useful tool to other people, just by pointing them to useful resources. This can take the form of an e-book, a web page, or even an [email newsletter](https://thewritelife.com/earn-money-through-substack/).

You don't need to be a web developer, a professional coder, or even a good writer. Anyone in a position to know **a little more** than the average person is able to put together a list of resources that cuts to the chase, gets past the noise, and guides others to where they want to go.

# Curation is as much a service as creation

A museum curator is never going to be applauded as much as the artist. However, the curator knew how to put the artist's work in a context that would delight and inform the museumgoer. The curator tells a story, and it's as much of a service as the person that created the work. By curating, you can put things in a useful context, and allow others to get right to the best parts, without having to slog through the petabytes of useless, rehashed crap that can be found on the internet.

**Creators offer novelty. Curators offer clarity.**

title: Innovation Leapfrogging
tldr: Technology is changing, and urban planning is going to get leapfrogged. In the next 20 years certain things that were incredibly important may become irrelevant.
md:
---
title: "Innovation Leapfrogging"
date: 2020-10-08
tldr: "Technology is changing, and urban planning is going to get leapfrogged. In the next 20 years certain things that were incredibly important may become irrelevant."
notion_id: c6d4c645-c2ee-4b7d-ac33-300793b60088
---

- Starlink is going to begin their [public beta](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2020/10/spacex-has-launched-enough-satellites-for-starlinks-upcoming-public-beta/) soon.

- Drone taxis are [in development](https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-aviation-volocopter/air-taxi-firm-volocopter-teams-up-with-schenker-to-deploy-heavy-lift-drones-idUKKCN26C0ST).

- High speed [electrical planes](https://www.rolls-royce.com/innovation/key-demonstrators/accel.aspx) are becoming available.

What does this all mean? 

Things are going to change, very quickly.

In 2015, [more people in India had access to smartphones than toilets](https://blogs.worldbank.org/opendata/are-cell-phones-becoming-more-popular-toilets). While this news bit was usually presented in the context of needing more sanitation, it can also be seen in another light: Innovation leapfrogging.

When innovation happens, it usually happens on the back of previous innovation.

Take indoor plumbing, for example. To have a workable, flushable toilet in a city, you have to have:

- Plumbing inside the house, connected to...

- a city sewage system, which leads to...

- a water treatment plant in the city, managed by...

- a working city government.

That's a lot of stacks. Take, for example, a smartphone:

- Electricity

- A cell network (Optional)

When you can remove the requirements for new technology, you can have rapid growth in a place that might lack things that we consider to be part of "civilized society".

Starlink is going to allow for high speed internet in the most remote places. This creates opportunities for knowledge workers to be as productive as anyone in the middle of a big tech hub. 

This now allows for certain things to be optional, like:

- City infrastructure

- Physical office space

- Proximity to your workplace

Drones are being developed at a breakneck speed. We're already experimenting with drone delivery, and aren't too far away from having people moved around in drones. This does something incredible: It makes roads optional, and eliminates geographical challenges in urban areas.

![](../assets/posts/innovation-leapfrogging/0332acbd-Untitled.png)

Monterrey, Mexico is a city built in between mountains and hills. What would be 10 minutes as-the-crow-flies is now a multi-hour car ride.

Imagine if those hills didn't matter anymore.

Imagine if living on those hills were now possible.

Imagine if you didn't need to save space for roads anymore.

Technology is changing, and urban planning is going to get leapfrogged. In the next 20 years certain things that were incredibly important (like interstates) may become irrelevant. What used to take decades to build up, can now be implemented in months. Little out-of-the-way towns can become tech hubs without warning. Knowledge workers can move away from high-price urban centers to rural parts of the world that offer low crime, cheap housing, and quality of life.

## My prediction?

- The importance of nations are going to give way to coalitions of cities (Think ancient greek city-states).

- New, important cities can pop up anywhere, since geography won't be as big a problem as they were before.

- Flight will become extremely cheap, and the hub-and-spoke model of air travel will give way to one-off Uber-style trips.

- Personal flight will finally become viable, because everything can be automated away.

- Most travel will be optional (though still important), since high-speed internet will reduce the need for in-person communication for knowledge work.

title: Slapping babies and coding
tldr: With experience comes the ability to know what is important and what isn't.
md:
---
title: "Slapping babies and coding"
date: 2020-10-07
tldr: "With experience comes the ability to know what is important and what isn't."
notion_id: 6e38dbc3-9e0f-429b-bc6e-02e5c240b8ac
---

Newborn babies look incredibly fragile, and any kind of movement feels like they would break. Parents are very gentle with their newborn babies, mostly because they don't want to do anything that would hurt their tiny baby.

Compare that with the doctors, nurses and attendants that handle babies all day long. They'll grab the baby by the legs, slap it on the butt, move it around without too much of a problem, and handle the child in ways parents wouldn't dream of doing.

To the untrained eye, it might look like carelessness. Don't they know that you have to be careful around babies?! However, they're being extremely careful. *They just know what matters and what doesn't.*

Babies, for example have weak necks, but a relatively strong spine. You can move them around by the legs and even hang them upside down, because as long as you don't mess with their neck, they're ok. Full term babies' skin is much more resilient than premature babies' skin. So while you would limit your handling of a preemie, you shouldn't have too much of a problem with a full-term baby.

To parents, however EVERYTHING IS FRAGILE PROCEED WITH CAUTION.

## Computers & Coding

This behavior isn't limited to new parents. I used to have lots of fun with my grandmother's computer, clearing cache, deleting unused folders, and stopping certain programs from starting up on boot, while she stood behind me, white-knuckled and saying "BE CAREFUL DON'T BREAK ANYTHING".

Web development is all about learning how to interact with the code in a way to get the results you want. An unexperienced person will look through a tutorial or article, and think that if they don't put the code in the EXACT order they found it, they'll break something. But someone who has gotten his hands dirty and experimented with the code knows what's important and what isn't.

- Does the order of the properties in an HTML tag matter? Not really — feel free to swap 'em around.

- Does the order of the values in a CSS shorthand property matter? Yes, so be careful.

As you get better and feel more comfortable working in the code, you'll learn that it's OK to move things around — you're not going to break anything (and if you do, hopefully you can start over). However, it's important to make the distinction: the goal isn't to become careless, it's to learn what things need extra care, and what things don't.

title: Friction
tldr: In order to do something that becomes part of your routine, remove all friction and focus on that ONE thing singlemindedly. Let everything else fall into place in its own time.
md:
---
title: "Friction"
date: 2020-10-06
tldr: "In order to do something that becomes part of your routine, remove all friction and focus on that ONE thing singlemindedly. Let everything else fall into place in its own time."
notion_id: a1c2a104-014c-4b33-8eb1-b8bf4426681d
---

It's easy to [write about consistency](/c5b136fe99264c378d79974b362a21e4), it's hard to be consistent.

I've moved my platform to Notion. Why?

Because the main thing I've wanted to do is get into the habit of writing. What has been keeping me from doing that?

Friction.

Friction when it comes to creating the post, moving it to markdown, and deploying.

I know how to develop, and design. That's not the problem. The problem is that I haven't been able to get into the groove of simply writing, due to the additional friction I've created for myself by using other platforms.

**What do I lose?** Lots of stuff.

- I lose SEO

- I lose control over layout

- I lose the ability to schedule posts

**What do I gain?**

- Exclusive focus on content

*And that makes all the difference.*

## The takeaway

Charles Duhigg writes about "keystone habits" in his book "[The Power of Habit](https://www.amazon.com/Power-Habit-What-Life-Business/dp/081298160X)". A keystone habit is one that hooks in a bunch of other habits that eventually change lots of other habits. In his book, he highlights a new CEO that prioritized safety over everything else. As a CEO, there are LOTS of things to think about other than safety, things like profitability and hiring and workplace culture. However, by focusing single-mindedly on safety, the CEO was able to upgrade machinery, improve processes, and build a culture that attracted high-quality hires. His single-minded focus ended up impacting every area of the company. The result is a profitable, healthy company.

In order to do something that becomes part of your routine, remove all friction and focus on that ONE thing single-mindedly. Let everything else fall into place in its own time.

*That's what I'm going to attempt.*

title: Listen, Understand, Empathize, Talk
md:
---
title: "Listen, Understand, Empathize, Talk"
date: 2020-05-18
notion_id: 8986cdea-d26c-41a0-9d0e-c1ada6688116
---

There's been a lot of debate on health lately. Everyone seems to have become expert epidemiologists, sociologists, statisticians, immunologists, and nutritionists. There are the "vaxxers" and "antivaxxers", the "Independent news" and "Mainstream Media", and everyone seems to be talking past each other.

Of course, everyone thinks that their cause is noble: to reveal the truth to the poor sheeple that are on the other side.

Here's a time saver for you: There is no article, blog post, podcast or youtube video that will convince the person to abandon ship and come to your life raft of truth and reason.

Why? **Because there is an underlying philosophy that needs to be addressed.**

I'm not going to try to advocate one side or the other, but I'd like to explore two different philosophies that have been clashing lately: the Integrated and the Systems philosophies.

I'm just making these terms up, even though there's probably actual terms out there, because they're already loaded in your mind. Let me try to define these two philosophies as best as possible. When I define them, I want to define them in ways that people from either side would agree with — I'm not interested in building up strawmen.

## Integrated Philosophy

This is the person that talks about "building up the immune system". They look for "natural" remedies, and are deeply suspicious of "traditional medicine". The term "Big Pharma" is used derisively in this crowd.

The basic idea is this: **The body knows best**.

For those that come from a theistic background, it's because God has created the body with all of the tools it needs to fight off any health threat.

For those that come from an evolutionistic background, it's because humans are the result of billions of years of evolution, perfectly fine-tuned to adapt to any kind of threat.

The Integrated Philosophy sees the human being as a unit of irreducible complexity, that is connected to the rest of the universe through nature — that is why natural remedies are best, since they work with the existing connections between nature and human.

The Integrated philosophy sees things like vaccines as an interruption of the natural order. God/Evolution/Whatever created a way for humans to interact with the natural world, and sticking a needle into your body hijacks that way of working, and sets off a chain reaction of problems inside of the human body.

## Systems Philosophy

A person that follows Systems Philosophy is most likely connected to a traditional system of education & healthcare. 

The basic idea is this: **It's systems all the way down.**

The body is made of organs, which are made of cells, which are made of proteins which are made of chemicals. They can be studied, tweaked, and fixed.

The scientific method works, and it needs to be followed and respected. Systems Philosophy understands the human body as many different systems that can be understood. Through science and technology, we've identified the parts of humans that can break down, and by taking research to the molecular level, we can create treatments for whatever is ailing the person. There are no atheists in foxholes, and there are no homeopaths with exposed fractures.

Systems philosophy sees things like vaccines like a scientific solution to the chaotic world of disease and infection. Plumbing cured Cholera, and vaccines eliminated Polio. Human advancement can be messy and take wrong turns, but in the long run, we progress as a species when we learn about the systems that exist in the body, identify the breakpoints, and work to solve it.

## What's the point of this?

How'd I do? Do you fall into one of the camps? Did I describe it accurately?

It's important to understand that for any issue, there is a person on the other side that has thought out the issue, and come to a conclusion. The first thing that needs to happen is that you have to **Listen, **not for the goal of responding, but to be able to **Understand** where the other person is coming from. Try to get an idea of the basic philosophy behind the argument. From there, move to **Empathizing**, - "I can see how, if you see the world in that way, how you'd come to the conclusion you did." Finally, and only after having passed those three steps, will ANYTHING you have to say make any difference in the mind of the other person. That's when you **talk**.

So, let's stop fooling ourselves into thinking that our post or article share is going to "wake up the sheeple", and let's start asking the "sheeple" what they think, and why they think the way they do. "Do YoUr ReSeArCH" doesn't quite cut it either. The research will be accepted or rejected based on the underlying philosophy they've come to believe, and until that's not addressed, there will never be a change.

title: The Simple Machines of the Internet
md:
---
title: "The Simple Machines of the Internet"
date: 2020-05-03
notion_id: 2fee4f1d-5e09-4b9c-b2f4-68605d80fc3c
---

In engineering, there are six "simple machines". They're defined as "as the simplest mechanisms that use mechanical advantage (also called leverage) to multiply force." They are:

- [Lever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lever)

- [Wheel and axle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheel_and_axle)

- [Pulley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulley)

- [Inclined plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclined_plane)

- [Wedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedge_(mechanical_device))

- [Screw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screw_(simple_machine))

With these simple machines, you can easily become more efficient in your work. Combining them makes them even more efficient

## Internet Simple Machines

At its most basic level, the internet connects things. There are basic categories to connection needs that can be combined to create even better online tools. They're not really "simple machines" in a mechanical sense — think of them more like robots (or [demons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daemon_(computing))). Although there might be more, i've defined the internet's simple machines as the following: 

## The Bouncer

Access control. This guy decides who comes in and goes out based on the conditions you gave it.

It's basically a login.

## The Scout

This is information retrieval and collection. It's the thing that hits an API for the weather and displays it. It's the stock ticker.

## The Number Cruncher

The Number Cruncher is a computer in a classical sense — something that computes.

It's the little form that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit, the thing that tells you [if it's Christmas](https://isitchristmas.com/).

## The Messenger

It facilitates connection between two people. Could be a contact form, a chatroom — whatever. Anything that makes two people able to communicate more efficiently.

Combinations of these things create value.

For example, a marketplace like Amazon is a communication tool, a retrieval tool and an access tool. With an account (bouncer), you get a listout of vendors (scout), and can transact with them (messenger).

### What about exchanging money?

Buying and selling online is an extremely complicated process, so a lot of it has been black-boxed by companies that facilitate payments, like Stripe, Paypal and Gumroad. It looks simple to us, but behind the scenes there's a lot going on. In fact, a lot of what we're doing when we set up a payment portal is building a scout to do an API call to our favorite service, and having the number cruncher calculate prices on our end, and send that information along. Then the rules will be passed to the Bouncer to give access to whatever we had behind our paywall, or passed to a Messenger to alert the seller that a sale has completed.

### Why does this matter?

To the user, this isn't very important. But as a creator, I want to explore new frameworks and languages beyond simple tutorials that take me down a set path of how to build a todo app or whatever. By learning how to make these four machines, I can instantly get value out of what I'm building, just like engineers can get value immediately from implementing simple machines into what they're building. So by understanding how access control works, how data collection works, how business logic and communication works, I'll have the building blocks for my next project.

title: Sharing isn't caring
md:
---
title: "Sharing isn't caring"
date: 2020-04-09
notion_id: a3dea4be-008d-4501-bc62-0c0de1353f87
---

I've done it. You've probably done it.

You have something really great that you want to put into the world, or some important news that you want to get across, or there's a cause you're passionate about, and you want everyone to be a part.

So you go to a social media platform and craft a beautiful post. It's incredible — with a captivating intro, a moving description, and a heartfelt call to action.

And then, the shares come:

"John shared this".

"Mary shared this"

"Silvia shared this"

The notifications are making your phone sing, and you're thinking, "This is it! We're REACHING PEOPLE!" Your marketing strategy worked perfectly!

But then, you wait for the signups, for the donations, for the customers.

Crickets.

Lots of eyeballs, but no real engagement.

## What happened?

Having someone share something to their own network of followers seems, in theory, to be a great way to get people to learn about your new product or project. "It's the network effect! It's viral!"

Unfortunately it rarely works out that way. Why not? I've got a few theories:

### Virtue Signaling

"Virtue Signaling" is a term that describes the outward actions of someone that is trying show virtuous character. It's not a new concept — here's how Jesus described the virtue signalers of his day:

> And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward.

—Matthew 6:5

Virtue signalling is the reason people want their electric cars to "look" eco-friendly (Prius, anyone?), even though there are plug-ins or hybrids that look exactly like the normal car model.

It's the reason people do video chats in front of their bookcase ("I have many leather-bound books and my apartment smells of rich mahogany.")

It's probably the reason they shared your post.

In other words, it's not really about you. By sharing your content, the sharer was able to communicate something about themselves ("Look, I support small businesses!" "Check it out, I'm socially conscious!" "I want you to think I donated!")

### The Bystander Effect

The Bystander Effect is what happens in videoconfrence meetings when the host asks, "so, what does everyone think? Does anyone have a question?", and there are blank stares all around.

There may be questions or comments, but everyone thinks that someone ELSE will engage. Meanwhile, they'll keep themselves on mute and take another bite of their sandwich.

[https://www.youtube.com/embed/4pQIpZr7xSI](https://www.youtube.com/embed/4pQIpZr7xSI)

The Bystander Effect happens in social media, too. Someone shares content, thinking "surely SOMEONE'S got to do SOMETHING. I'll pass on the info" 

## What to do?

Maybe this has been your experience - how do you put content out into the world in a way that ACTUALLY impacts?

### Make it about selfish generosity

When someone shares your content, they're either doing it to signal their virtue, or they're doing it as a favor to you. It's the reason your mom is the first one to share your stuff, even though she probably has no idea what it's about (hi mom!). 

Compare that with memes. No one cares who originally posted the meme - it's funny! In fact, the person sharing it isn't being generous to the original content creator, he's generously sharing it with his followers. He gets to be the hero in this story.

The question to ask yourself is: Does my content create actual value that will make the sharer seem like a generous person for having shared it?

#### PayPal & selfish generosity

Paypal took this to an [extreme](https://www.referralcandy.com/blog/paypal-referrals/) when they first started. They had a referral program that would pay each person $10 for a referral, and give away $10 to the new signups. Ten bucks for free? This made you look like a hero to all of your friends, while giving some value to the sharer. "Hey everyone, get on PayPal, I've got free money for you!"

So when you're creating the content you want to share, don't think about the people that will share it because they have a personal connection to you — think about how it will be valuable to the person that receives it. Any content that we create and distribute freely is a gift. Make sure that your gift has value.

### Put some skin in the game

Another possiblity is to encourage people not to mindlessly share things, but to share their experiences with others. It's the reason those horrible (but effective) [one-page marketing websites](https://pro.chooseyourselffinancial.com/p/ALR_sidehustle_ar_0219/WALRV703/Full?h=true) have so many testimonials — it's showing people actually using the product, and others to take part.

So if you want to get more people to visit your taco stand, don't just post something and hope others will share. Invite people to share their experience through a photo, a review, a testimonial. Make the message "I've tried it and loved it. I want you to try it too".

### Do it old-school

When getting certified to administer CPR, the trainers warn about the bystander effect. They get around it by suggesting that the person giving CPR point out someone in the crowd, and instead of saying "Someone call 9-1-1!", say "Hey! You in the red shirt and blue hat — call 9-1-1!"

A personal plea is always going to go way, WAY farther than a simple "share". 

So, if you really want to get your content out there, share it, one by one, with people that you think would appreciate it. You'll get more traction that way.

The next time you share something and it flops, don't take it personally. Go back, inject more value into your gift, see how you get people to actually show the value it was to THEM, and reach out to people personally - Go share your gift.

title: Black Boxes, Tractors & Ignorance
md:
---
title: "Black Boxes, Tractors & Ignorance"
date: 2020-04-08
notion_id: 07e35c21-3011-4252-a971-b8d7917bd0aa
---

** **Update: I've since moved to a hacky implementation of Notion, but my original point still stands **** 

At the time of this writing, the blog looks like crap.

It's on Github, it doesn't even have a decent URL (yet — i'm working on that), and I can't quite figure out how to change the profile picture.

Why would I put myself through this, when there are literally HUNDREDS of decent blogging platforms that actually work better?

First, a story about tractor hacking:

[https://www.youtube.com/embed/F8JCh0owT4w](https://www.youtube.com/embed/F8JCh0owT4w)

Apparently farmers that bought relatively modern tractors found themselves out of options when it came to repairs, because John Deere made it so that any repair had to be done by authorized John Deere technicians.

Which creates a question: when do you really own something? If there are things you can't do with your own property, is it really yours?

I don't want to get into the nuance about it, but it's safe to say that restrictions make something "less yours". You're not "sovereign" over the thing you supposedly own.

### Black Boxes

A "black box" is any part of a system that is obscured. You basically see it in terms of inputs and outputs. I give the black box something, and something spits out.

Sometimes it's intentionally obscured, like anything with a "secret recipe" (it's called "special sauce" because you have no idea what's in it).

Sometimes it's obscured because you just have no idea what's going on, like me whenever I pop the hood of my trunk. I give the car gas, and it lets me drive. The engine is pretty much a big black box to me. Input and output.

Black boxes create dependencies. Farmers need a John Deere tech to work on their tractor, even though they know how to do it. I need a mechanic to work on my car, because I don't know what I'm doing. 

### What does this have to do with a badly built blog?

I've used different blogging platforms, but I wanted to take ownership of what I was putting together. On Medium, you're putting your articles on a distribution service. They can take executive decisions regarding the platform, and they don't need your permission. 

On WordPress, the actual post sits on a WordPress-formatted database table entry. Moving, exporting, or changing platforms can get difficult. Also, WordPress is a system that I already know and understand. I wanted the challenge of getting my hands dirty in a react-based JS environment.

I wanted to intentionally do the hard thing of working on every aspect of the system, in order to know how it's all put together. In order to make it *really* mine.

I want to figure out how Gatsby's platform works, how routing is set up, how the markdown files are set up to display, how far I can stretch Github's free "pages" platform.

Because at the end of the day, the only thing you really own, the only thing no one can take away from you, are the lessons you learn.

title: Consistency > Quality
md:
---
title: "Consistency > Quality"
date: 2020-04-07
notion_id: c5b136fe-9926-4c37-8d79-974b362a21e4
---

[https://www.youtube.com/embed/R2_Mn-qRKjA](https://www.youtube.com/embed/R2_Mn-qRKjA)

Something happens every time I want to do something consistently — especially writing. I've got some ideas in the back of my pocket, and I want to start to put out content into the world.

And then, I run out of things to say. I don't want to write anymore.

I'm not the only one - It's actually a thing in startup world. They call it "The trough of sorrow". It's when the buzz and the initial enthusiasm wears off, and you realize that success is only going to come by checking in, doing the work, and being consistent.

[https://twitter.com/AdamJTPalmer/status/459688087178579968?s=20](https://twitter.com/AdamJTPalmer/status/459688087178579968?s=20)

No one likes to struggle through a routine that isn't fun anymore. No one likes to be intentional with something that doesn't captivate and enchant the way it used to. No one wants to put in the hours.

But everyone wants to have a book with their name on it.

Everyone wants to have done "something great".

Everyone wants that sculpted body, that sharp mind, that incredible skill.

Everyone wants the result of the hard work without actually doing it.

### So what do I do?

I don't know — I'm just writing this because I didn't post yesterday's until today! Go read a motivational blog, I'm asking the same questions you are, buddy.

In all seriousness — two things: One, go read a [post I wrote a while ago about habits](https://medium.com/@antar37/i-should-do-that-thing-more-4edc212cca71). I'm still struggling with this, so it's as much a reminder to me as it is a help to you.

Second, know that when your highest priority is consistency, you're not going to hit home runs every time. Some days it's going to be a bad workout, a bad article, a disappointing practice. That's OK, because you showed up, and did the work.

And for that, I applaud you.

title: Who gave you permission?
md:
---
title: "Who gave you permission?"
date: 2020-04-06
notion_id: c2308552-a423-4c11-afd6-3f028dace9a5
---

One of the things that stop people from writing is the idea of permission - A little idea in the back of your head that you're not "allowed" to write about a given topic, because you're not qualified, certified, or recognized. "**You don't belong**", is what the gatekeepers are saying.

### The most intimidating gatekeeper: yourself.

Most of the time no one needs to be guarding the door to a given topic or community, because it's the little voice in your head that's doing the hard work of making you feel disqualified.

The problem of qualification is that in order to produce quality work, you have to first make horrible work. There's really no way around it. Sometimes that horrible work happens in a closed environment (like the case of a university student learning how to design. Their terrible work is hidden behind the university walls), or it's done in the open (like a cover band that performs their terrible music in friends-and-family concerts). In my case, I'm dedicating myself to write in the open, and share it.

I'm reminded of this [quote](http://deltaskymag.com/Sky-Extras/Favorites/Rock--n--Roll-Jedi.aspx) by Dave Grohl:

> When I think about kids watching a TV show like *American Idol *or *The Voice*, then they think, ‘Oh, OK, that’s how you become a musician, you stand in line for eight f****** hours with 800 people at a convention center and then you sing your heart out for someone and then they tell you it’s not f****** good enough.’ Can you imagine?” he implores. “It’s destroying the next generation of musicians! Musicians should go to a yard sale and buy an old f****** drum set and get in their garage and just suck. And get their friends to come in and they’ll suck, too. And then they’ll f******* start playing and they’ll have the best time they’ve ever had in their lives and then all of a sudden they’ll become Nirvana. Because that’s exactly what happened with Nirvana. Just a bunch of guys that had some s***** old instruments and they got together and started playing some noisy-a** s***, and they became the biggest band in the world. That can happen again! You don’t need a f****** computer or the Internet or *The Voice *or *American Idol*.”

### Other gatekeepers: your competition

When do other people start to try to stop you from creating? When you start to get good enough to be a threat. That's when others will start nitpicking and taking apart your work, and try to get you to "stay in your lane". In a sense, it's a good thing. When people are actively trying to close the door on you, it's because you already got your foot in.

### The only real gatekeepers: your consumers

J.K Rowling, the only billionaire book author, got rejected by 12 publishing houses. She only got the green light when the 8-year-old daughter of a publishing house chairman read the first chapter and demanded the next one. 

So who are you creating for? Those are the people you answer to. If your consumers close the door on you, there's nothing else you can do.

As for that little voice in your head, don't shut it out completely. "This is terrible, you're not any good", it says. And that voice is most likely right. But it's also pointing to something else: that you know what you want, and you're not there yet.

Listen to this essay by Ira Glass (it's a famous one, so you've probably heard it before) on the gap between what you want, and what you're able to create in the moment.

[https://www.youtube.com/embed/X2wLP0izeJE](https://www.youtube.com/embed/X2wLP0izeJE)

What do you do with the external gatekeepers? Pay attention to them, too. But pay attention to the motive: The more intense the pushback becomes, the more of a threat you're becoming - so use their resistance as signposts.

So who gave you permission? No one. You have to give it to yourself, and get out there and make something crappy. Make it in private, make it in public, but understand that if you're not making something horrible, you'll never make something great.

title: There is no Wizard
tldr: At the end of the day, we're all making things up as we go, regardless of how structured things look. There is no Wizard of Oz - just a bumbling man behind the curtain.
md:
---
title: "There is no Wizard"
date: 2020-04-03
tldr: "At the end of the day, we're all making things up as we go, regardless of how structured things look. There is no Wizard of Oz - just a bumbling man behind the curtain."
notion_id: 0755f456-aa95-4117-ae5a-5771cb8353e9
---

> "I am Oz, the Great and the Terrible," the Voice said.
"Where are you, Great Oz?" Dorothy asked.
"I am everywhere," the Voice said. "What do you want?"
"You wanted me to kill the Wicked Witch," Dorothy said bravely. "Well, I have killed her. Now you must send me back to Kansas, as you promised."
"You promised me brains," said the Scarecrow.
"You promised me a heart," said the Tin Man.
"I was promised courage," said the Cowardly Lion.
"Did I make all those promises?" the Voice said. "Well, the Wicked Witch is dead! I must have time to think."
"But I want my courage NOW!" the Cowardly Lion said, "And I WILL have it!"
He was so angry that he gave a great roar. The roar was so frightening that Toto jumped away from him. The little dog knocked over the screen. Behind the screen was a little old man.
The Tin Man ran towards the man and raised his axe.
"Who are you?" the Tin Man cried. "Where is Oz?"
"I am Oz," the little old man said. "Please don't hit me.
People think that I am a Great Wizard, but I'm only a man."
"Then you are a HUMBUG" the Tin Man said. 
"You have told lies and deceived everyone for years."
Behind the screen was a little old man.
"Yes, that's right. I am a humbug," the little old man said.
"But you are the only people who know that. I know lots of
tricks I tricked you, didn't I?"

The Wizard of Oz, L. Frank Baum

![](../assets/posts/there-is-no-wizard/ca0d4d7f-Untitled.png)

In any organized institution there's a desire to create an illusion of control, and that everything has been thought through. The fearless leader has it all figured out, and if he or she goes in a certain direction, it's because it's been pored over, analyzed and masterfully planned out. This happens at all organizational levels, from families to multinational organizations. There's a need to create the idea that there is a great and powerful wizard of Oz behind everything. "It's all under control", they'll make you think.

- But I've seen pastors preach a sermon on the fly, changing the program in the act.

- I've seen multinational companies talk up a "new initiative" that was made up on a whim.

- Entire countries have pivoted because of a single idea, a moment, or a petty argument.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E9eAshaPvYw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E9eAshaPvYw)

If you have a chance, watch "The Death of Stalin" - a dark comedy based on the bumblings of the closest circle of Stalin's men. Although it feels bizarre, a lot of what was depicted is based in history.

### What does this mean?

With no Wizard of Oz wisely dictating what can and can't be done, go ahead and pitch the idea you've got. After all, who's to say the little man behind the curtain won't appreciate the input? At the end of the day, we're all making things up as we go, regardless of how structured things look. So try new things, look at the "bigger" players in your field in the eye, and know that if you're insecure and unsure, they probably feel the same way.

title: I Should Do That Thing More
md:
---
title: "I Should Do That Thing More"
date: 2019-03-25
notion_id: dd2b8fe1-270f-4bfd-b0cd-bdb3fbc0eb3f
---

I've been told I should write.

I've wanted to work out more.

I've wanted to program more.

I've wanted to do lots of stuff more, but I haven't "found the time".

I'm a terrible procrastinator, and I usually keep things on the backburner until I forget about them. 

However, I've been trying to get better. I'm using a habit tracker to quantify my habits (aiming for that 21-day streak!), and trying to get to a point where I've found the method to do more, and complain less about my not doing.

What's been my strategy?

## Daily goals should be clearly defined tasks that don't take more than ten minutes.

You don't want to get over-enthusiastic and create ten different daily goals that would effectively take several hours to complete... that's a part-time job, not a daily rhythm adjustment.

Keep your goals clearly defined, even though you're looking towards a bigger goal. For example, don't say "lose half a pound a week" as a goal. That's too broad. Something like "walk 10,000 steps" would be better, even though your END goal is to lose weight.

Keep things short. Think of the things that you absolutely HAVE to do every day (brush your teeth, take a shower, etc). They don't take very long. If you've got an everyday goal like "run", keep in mind that from getting ready to coming back from your run will eat up at least 30 minutes of your time. Combine that with 5 or 6 other goals you want to accomplish, and you're looking at 1.5 to 2 hours of daily tasks. 

## Start with things you kind of like, but aren't organized enough to be consistent with.

If you're looking to make your daily goal as natural as brushing your teeth, you should probably start with things you already enjoy doing. Otherwise, you'll quickly get frustrated and give up. Once you feel the VICTORY of turning a few goals into habits, you can move on to things you don't really enjoy. There are two reasons you need to intentionally track the daily goals you've chosen: One, you're a disorganized mess, and two, you lack the willpower to get through unenjoyable tasks. Work on your organization first, then tackle the unenjoyable stuff.

## Only ramp up once you have a 21-day streak

You need to prove to yourself that you can do this. So start slowly, and work your way up to new things. Get a streak in, and then ramp up. If your goal is getting fit, having something like "Do 30 pushups" would be a good goal. If after a while you're feeling ambitious and want to bump it up to 40 or 50, wait until you've got a solid streak at the previous amount (I'm not saying you shouldn't do more if you're up for it, — just don't hold yourself to a DAILY goal at that new, higher amount until you've hit a 21-day streak).

## Don't feel terrible if you fall off the wagon

You're trying to turn activities into habits - activities that aren't currently part of your daily rhythm. That's difficult. Not impossible, but difficult. Don't worry if you mess up or skip a couple of days. You might even need to put that particular habit on hold until you've worked up the willpower to tackle it (forming new habits — any habits — mold and grow your willpower)

## Know your rhythms

Some people want to work out EVERY DAY, but might have weekends that are particularly crazy, or might travel a lot and can't hit some of the goals in a different environment (you're not going to write a page of that novel you've been working on while you're in meetings all day).

So know your rhythm, and anticipate it. Mondays are crazy? Don't go out for your daily walk on Mondays — 6 days a week is fine. Weekends are very different from your weekend rhythm? Adjust — have weekday goals. In the end, it's about giving you the structure you need to get the results you want. A little bit at a time.

This article was written over the course of a week, following a weekday goal of "Write a paragraph".
